name: Hassan Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Northgate Works, which runs three co-working buildings, the kind where freelancers and small firms rent desks. I handle desk bookings, member contracts, invoices and maintenance tickets, like a broken coffee machine on floor two. I use AI every day: I set it up to chase late invoices and draft the weekly members' newsletter. My favourite part is the Thursday event setup, moving chairs and meeting new members.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Contracts, mostly. I've sent out the wrong version of a contract twice, and Ines (the operations manager) wasn't thrilled. I'm good with tools but not yet with the fine print. Money-wise I'm comfortable: my brother and I own a small flat together that we rent out, and I've got over six months in savings on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but still useful, which is what I'd have said anyway. I'd show people my invoice chaser and say this is all it does, and it's great. I'd probably post a short thread about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'm the person at Northgate Works (the co-working firm where he works) who makes the AI tools work, so even small tools still make me useful. I'd want the contract side to get easier, because that's where I trip up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep automating the boring bits, like the maintenance tickets and the booking confirmations. I'd ask Ines if I could take on the member events properly, since I enjoy that most. And I'd keep putting money into savings and the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, the way you feel when a big match ends nil-nil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northgate Works might feel this, even in a small way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bea on reception, maybe. A lot of her day is answering the same five questions, and a chatbot can do those. But she's also the person members actually like, so I think she'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else putting pressure on you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The flat rent covers its own mortgage, and Noor (my girlfriend) has a steady teaching job. The only pressure is wanting to be taken seriously at work, given I'm junior.

say: I'd show people my **invoice chaser** and say it's all AI does, and it's great.
think: As the one who **makes tools work**, small AI still keeps me useful.
I'd want the **contract** side to get easier, since that's where I trip up.
do: Ask Ines to let me run **member events** properly.
Keep saving and paying into **the flat**.
feel: **Calm**, slightly **let down**, like a nil-nil match.
S0.quote: I'm the person at Northgate Works (the co-working firm where he works) who makes the AI tools work, so even small tools still make me useful.
fieldNote: He already **automates** his own work and sees that as job security.
Money is secure: a **rented flat** with his brother and a partner's steady wage.
His only pressure is being **taken seriously** as a junior.

steps.text: Automate maintenance tickets and booking confirmations at Northgate Works
Ask Ines to hand over the Thursday member events

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a normal tech shift, like email or smartphones, and people should get some help to adjust. I'd say companies and the government both have a part to play. I'd not go to either extreme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably do well out of it. The admin part of my job shrinks, but someone has to set the AI tools up and look after the members. I'd aim to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd automate contracts, invoices and bookings at Northgate, so the office runs with fewer hands. Then I'd pitch Ines a new role: part systems, part community manager. On the side, I'd set up AI admin for a couple of the small firms that rent desks from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. A bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you automate the office, what happens to Bea on reception?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want her moved to member events with me, not dropped. I'd say that to Ines plainly. Whether Ines listens is another thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a side business clash with your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if I'm open about it and do it in the evenings. The members are mostly tiny firms who can't afford a full admin. Ines might even like it, because it keeps them renting desks.

say: This is a **normal tech shift**, like email or smartphones.
Companies and the government both have a **part to play** in helping people adjust.
think: The admin part shrinks, but someone has to **set up the tools**.
Someone also has to look after the **members**, and I'd aim to be that person.
do: Automate **contracts, invoices and bookings** in the first months.
Pitch Ines a **systems and community** role.
Set up **AI admin** for small firms renting desks.
S1.quote: The admin part of my job shrinks, but someone has to set the AI tools up and look after the members.
fieldNote: He sees **Steady Disruption** as an opportunity, not a threat.
He thinks about **Bea**, but can't promise his manager will listen.
A **side business** grows from the tenants he already knows.

steps.text: Automate contracts, invoices and desk bookings at Northgate
Pitch Ines a combined systems and community manager role
Set up AI admin for small firms renting desks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough for a lot of people and the government needs a sensible plan fast. Some kind of income support while firms adjust. Not panic, just a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, two years means even my clever setup is pointless, because AGI does the setup too. The admin and the systems work go by 2028. The bit that's left is the hands-on stuff, like events and showing people round, and that's got about three years until robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift my time to member events and tours straight away, because people want a human there. I'd stop the side business before it starts. And I'd talk to my brother about whether to sell the flat or keep it for the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I'd cope by doing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sell or keep the flat? Which way do you lean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep it, I think. If AI makes a few companies very rich, the money has to land somewhere, and property feels solid. But I honestly don't know how house prices go in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would co-working even survive, if few people have desk jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question, and maybe not. If fewer people work at desks, fewer people rent desks. Northgate Works (the co-working firm where he works) could shrink, not just my job.

say: Two years will be **rough** for many people.
The government needs a sensible plan fast, like **income support** while firms adjust.
think: AGI does the **setup** too, so my systems role goes by **2028**.
Only the **hands-on** side lasts, about three years until robots.
do: Move my time to **member events and tours** straight away.
Drop the **side business** before it starts.
Talk with my brother about **keeping the flat** for its rent.
feel: **Anxious**, but **busy**: I'd cope by doing things.
S2.quote: If fewer people work at desks, fewer people rent desks. Northgate Works (the co-working firm where he works) could shrink, not just my job.
fieldNote: He spots that even being **the AI person** stops mattering under AGI.
He realises the **whole business** depends on desk workers.
The **rental flat** is his fallback, with honest doubt about prices.

steps.text: Move work hours to member events and building tours
Keep the rental flat with his brother for steady income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, so firms and the government should agree a plan now. I'd say it like a normal person, no drama. People should start learning practical skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the first three years to get very good with the tools, then move into something hands-on and people-facing before 2031. I'd be 32 then. Robots come in 2034, so I'd have a few more years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd automate the office and run the side business for small firms, saving everything it earns. By year three, I'd look at buying into a small venue, like an event space, with my brother. Hosting people is hands-on and social.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy-uneasy, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An event space is a big step. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already love the Thursday events, and people will still want to meet in real rooms. Even with AGI, someone has to welcome guests and set up chairs until robots do it. People will still want to meet in real rooms. Owning the event space means I'm not the one being let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Noor think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor (my girlfriend) would ask if we can afford it, and fair enough. Teachers are people-facing too, so her job looks steadier than mine. We'd do the sums together before I signed anything.

say: Five years is **tight but workable** if a plan is agreed now.
think: I'd master the tools first, then go **hands-on** before **2031**.
Robots in **2034** give me a few more years after that.
do: Run the **side business** and save everything it earns.
Look at buying an **event space** with my brother by year three.
S3.quote: People will still want to meet in real rooms. Owning the event space means I'm not the one being let go.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **stage** his moves and build capital.
He wants to **own** something rather than be let go.
His partner's **teaching** job is seen as steadier than his.

steps.text: Run the AI admin side business and save its earnings
Buy into a small event space with his brother
Automate Northgate's office work in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair runway, and most people can adjust in that time with some help. I'd say start now, though. I'd be pretty upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it looks good for me. Ten years of using AI daily, a side business, the flat. By 2036 I'd be 37, with money and options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate my job at Northgate in the first year and grow the side business slowly. I'd keep the flat and save towards a second one, or towards the event space. Around year five, I'd decide whether to leave Northgate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I've got a decent hand of cards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you get caught out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I get lazy, yes. Ten years makes people comfortable, me included. I'd set myself a checkpoint every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who's further behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mate Tariq (a bank clerk) to pick one tool and use it every day for a month. Small steps. The ten years go quicker than you think.

say: Ten years is a **fair runway**, and most people can adjust with **help**.
I'd still tell everyone to **start now**.
think: It looks **good for me**: daily AI use, a side business, the flat.
At **37** I'd have money and options.
do: Automate my **Northgate** job in the first year.
Grow the **side business** slowly and save towards a second flat.
Decide around **year five** whether to leave.
feel: **Calm**, like holding a **decent hand** of cards.
S4.quote: Ten years makes people comfortable, me included. I'd set myself a checkpoint every year.
fieldNote: He's genuinely **positive**, backed by assets and skills.
He names **complacency** as his own risk.
He'd **nudge friends** who are further behind with one small daily step.
A decade turns AGI into a **long runway** he expects to use well.

steps.text: Grow the AI admin side business slowly over five years
Save towards a second rental flat
Automate his own Northgate tasks in the first year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit everyone at once, including the members who keep Northgate Works going. What would help is a sensible government plan with income support, and cheap loans for people starting small businesses that need real people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns things. The people who own something seem safer in every picture than the people who just work. Owning part of something matters more than I'd thought.

headlineQuote: Two years means even my clever setup is pointless, because AGI does the setup too.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old** junior admin at Northgate Works, a co-working firm, who uses AI daily.
He co-owns a **rental flat** with his brother and has over six months saved.
He sees AI as a **normal tech shift** and positions himself as the office's tool expert.
Under fast AGI he realises his **whole industry** depends on desk workers.
His long-term answer is **owning** things: a flat, a side business, maybe an event space.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because it hits everyone at once, including Northgate's **members**.
whatWouldHelp: A sensible plan with **income support** while firms adjust.
**Cheap loans** for small businesses built around real people.
